newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK inflation stubbornly above target in Jan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK inflation stubbornly above target in Jan.

text.p: Britain's core rate of inflation stuck stubbornly at 3.1 percent in January, official data showed on Thursday, adding weight to the Bank of England's call for a swift rise in interest rates to keep price pressures in check.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said core inflation, which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments, fell 0.2 percent in the month, but the annual rate was unchanged from December.
This leaves inflation stubbornly above the government's target of 2.5 percent which it originally aimed to hit before the election, due by May.
But the government insisted inflation would soon edge lower.

"Serious commentators, including the Bank of England in their Inflation Report yesterday, expect inflation to fall back over the coming months," Angela Knight, economic secretary to Britain's Treasury, said in a statement.
"The strength of sterling and this week's excellent producer price figures show inflation remains under firm control."
Headline annual inflation rose to 2.8 percent in January, its highest level for a year, from 2.5 percent in December.

City economists had expected core inflation to edge lower to 3.0 percent and the headline figure to edge up to 2.7 percent. They said the figures would help endorse the central bank's call for an immediate quarter point interest rate rise.
"This gives a little more credence to the Bank of England's view that we should see a small tightening in monetary policy in the near future," said Philip Uglow, UK economist at Union plc.
The figures come a day after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke dismissed the Bank's call for higher interest rates to keep price pressures under control.

Setting out its case in a key speech on Tuesday and the quarterly inflation report on Wednesday, the Bank said rates needed to rise immediately by a quarter point to ensure the government hit its inflation target in the medium term.
If rates were left unchanged, inflation would pick up to around 3.0 percent or more within two years, the Bank said.
But Clarke said he had no intention of checking economic growth by raising the cost of borrowing.
"I think it is not yet at the stage where I have to put the brakes on," he said in a radio interview.

Britain is enjoying the lowest inflation for 30 years, but its track record is poor and economists are suspicious that political considerations still outweigh economic arguments when it comes to interest rate moves.
With an election only months away, they think it highly unlikely Clarke would sanction an unpopular interest rate rise which would hit millions of home owners.

"The odds are really stacked against a rate rise now," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders. "If the election was not fast approaching I'm sure Clarke would have given in and raised them again."
